analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal tax credit that lets corporations avoid tax on profits earned in Puerto Rico.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, it never received a markup, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and expired when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1921, section 936 of the tax code has let U.S. companies operating in Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories pay essentially no federal income tax on the profits they earn there. This bill would have repealed that credit entirely, starting with tax years after 1993, so those profits would be taxed like profits earned anywhere else. Repealing it would have raised federal revenue from some of the largest U.S. corporations, most famously drug manufacturers that ran their production in Puerto Rico partly for the tax break. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, because a corporate tax break costing the Treasury billions of dollars a year would be ended, with the money available for other priorities or deficit reduction. Mainland-based competitors of territory-based companies would also face a more level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 936 of the Internal Revenue Code in full, ending the Puerto Rico and possession tax credit for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993 [S3].

The credit lets U.S. corporations pay no federal income tax on income from operations in Puerto Rico and other U.S. possessions, so repeal would return that untaxed profit to the federal tax base [S2].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. corporations with operations in Puerto Rico and the territories, above all pharmaceutical and other manufacturers that located production there to shelter profits from federal tax; Puerto Rico's economy, which had used the credit to attract factories and jobs, would also bear costs.

drawbacks.text: Puerto Rico had built a manufacturing base on the promise of the section 936 credit; full repeal with no replacement, as this bill proposed, could cost the island jobs and investment, an effect that hits U.S. citizens in Puerto Rico directly [S3].
An abrupt full repeal, rather than a phase-down or a redesigned credit, gives companies little time to adjust where they produce, an objection an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: closing a decades-old corporate tax shelter raises federal revenue and ends an expensive distortion that rewards booking profit in a territory rather than making goods more efficiently. But the bill's blunt approach was a genuine weakness — full repeal with no transition and no substitute for Puerto Rico's job-attraction incentive would risk real harm to the island's workers. A better-designed version would pair repeal with a wage-based alternative and a phase-in; Congress in fact later took that more careful path, but this bill did not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Jim Cooper introduced the bill on August 4, 1993 and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The corporations that used the section 936 credit — especially drug and other manufacturers operating in Puerto Rico — kept a federal tax exemption worth billions of dollars a year because Congress never acted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations using the Puerto Rico tax credit

industries.note: Drug companies famously located production in Puerto Rico under the section 936 credit, which let them bring home territory profits free of federal tax; repeal would have ended one of the largest corporate tax shelters of the era [S2][S3]. The cost of keeping the shelter was federal revenue that ordinary taxpayers otherwise would not have to make up.

industries.industry: U.S. corporations with Puerto Rico and territorial operations
industries.note: Any U.S. company earning income in Puerto Rico or other possessions paid essentially no federal income tax on it under section 936; the bill would have taxed those profits like mainland profits [S2][S3].

The credit was Puerto Rico's main tool for attracting factories and jobs, so full repeal could cost island workers employment; those same workers were U.S. citizens whose island's tax-driven development strategy came at federal revenue's expense [S3].
